passages.happening:
God sends Jeremiah down to the potter's house (verse 2). He watches the potter at the wheel. ‘But the vessel that he was shaping from the clay became flawed in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do’ (verse 4).

God asks whether he cannot do with Israel as the potter does with the clay. ‘Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel’ (verse 6). If God announces that a nation will be uprooted, ‘But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring’ (verse 8). And if he announces that he will build up a nation, but it does evil, he will relent of the good he intended (verses 9 and 10).

So Jeremiah is to tell Judah that God is shaping disaster against them, and to call each one to turn from his evil way (verse 11). But they answer that it is hopeless; they will follow their own plans and the stubbornness of their hearts (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Potters were among the most common craftsmen in any town, and broken pottery is the most common find in the land's ancient sites. The wheel was usually two stone discs on a pivot, the lower one kept turning while the potter shaped the clay on the upper. If the clay had a flaw, such as a stone or an air pocket, the potter squashed it down and began again.

The lesson cuts two ways. God is free, as a potter is free. But his freedom is not cold. He responds to what the clay does. A nation warned of judgment can turn and be spared, as Nineveh was in Jonah's day. A nation promised good can turn to evil and lose it.

Judah's answer in verse 12 is despair dressed as defiance. It is hopeless, they say, so they will go their own way.
passages.later: When Nineveh turned, ‘He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them’ (Jonah 3:10). Paul uses the potter's right over the clay in his own argument: ‘Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel’ for different uses? (Romans 9:21).
passages.asks: God says a nation that turns can be reshaped. Ask what in your life God might reshape if you let him. And ask whether you have ever said it is hopeless as a way of refusing to change.

passages.t: Does the snow of Lebanon fail?
passages.happening:
God tells them to ask among the nations whether anyone has heard of such a thing: ‘Virgin Israel has done a most terrible thing’ (verse 13). ‘Does the snow of Lebanon ever leave its rocky slopes?’ (verse 14). Do its cool streams ever run dry? ‘Yet My people have forgotten Me’ (verse 15). They burn incense to worthless idols that make them stumble off the ancient roads onto rutted byways (verse 15).

Their land will be a desolation, and passers-by will shake their heads (verse 16). God will scatter them like the east wind and show them his back, not his face, in the day of their disaster (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The snow of Lebanon's high peaks lasts much of the year, and the streams fed by it run cold even in summer. Nature keeps faith. God's people do not.

The ancient roads were the old, well-made ways, and the byways rutted tracks where travelers stumble. The picture matches the call to the ancient paths in chapter 6.

To show the back and not the face is the opposite of the priests' prayer in Numbers 6, which asked God to make his face shine on his people.
passages.later: Jeremiah had already called the people to ‘Ask for the ancient paths’ (Jeremiah 6:16). Aaron's prayer asked the reverse of verse 17: ‘may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you’ (Numbers 6:25).
passages.asks: The snow of Lebanon does not fail, but God's people forgot him. Ask what in creation keeps faith more steadily than you do. And ask which rutted byway you have taken off the old road.

passages.t: A pit dug for the prophet, and a harsh prayer
passages.happening:
Some say, ‘Come, let us make plans against Jeremiah’ (verse 18), for the law will never be lost to the priest, nor counsel to the wise, nor a word to the prophet. They plan to attack him with their tongues and pay no attention to his words (verse 18).

Jeremiah prays. “Attend to me, O LORD. Hear what my accusers are saying!” (verse 19). ‘Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for me’ (verse 20). He reminds God how he stood before him to speak good on their behalf and turn his anger away (verse 20).

Then his prayer turns harsh. He asks God to hand their children over to famine and the sword, and their wives to be widowed (verse 21). Let a cry be heard from their houses, for they dug a pit to catch him (verse 22). God knows all their deadly plots; he asks God not to forgive them (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
This is the fourth of Jeremiah's confessions. His enemies were the religious leaders: priests, the wise and the prophets. They were sure that God's word would never leave them, so they did not need Jeremiah's.

Their plan to strike him with the tongue means accusations and slander. The pit is a picture of a trap, and later in the book Jeremiah is lowered into a real one.

The prayer of verses 21 to 23 is among the harshest words in any prophet's mouth. Jeremiah had prayed for these people. Now they were trying to kill him, and he pours out his rage to God.
passages.later: A psalm prays in the same way against those who repaid good with evil (Psalm 109:5). Jesus taught, ‘love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you’ (Matthew 5:44).
passages.hard:
How can a prophet of God pray for his enemies' children to starve and their husbands to die?

Verses 21 to 23 belong to a kind of prayer called imprecation, found also in Psalms such as 69, 109 and 137. Several things help a reader. Jeremiah does not take revenge; he hands the case to God, the judge who knows their deadly plots. What he asks for is the very judgment God had already announced on the city, so he is asking God to carry out his declared justice against people trying to kill his messenger. And the prayer is honest: Scripture records the rage of a man betrayed after praying for his attackers, rather than hiding it.

Interpreters differ on whether to read the prayer as a model or as a faithful record of a suffering man's words that God then answers in his own way. Christians read it in light of Jesus' command to love enemies, which does not deny the longing for justice but hands it wholly to God (Romans 12:19). The prayer gives no one a warrant to wish harm on anyone's children.
passages.asks: Jeremiah brought his rage to God instead of acting on it. Ask what anger you are carrying, and whether you have brought it to God. And ask whom you could begin to pray for, as Jesus taught, even if you are not there yet.
